title: Oxidation states and naming; Oxidation states and half-equations
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RX02#t3 term and clue written for the game; RX02#t2 term and clue written for the game; RX02#t1 term and clue written for the game; RX01#t1 term and clue written for the game. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Metal hydride
items.clue: Compound such as NaH or CaH₂ in which H is −1.

items.label: Peroxide
items.clue: Compound such as H₂O₂ or Na₂O₂ in which O is −1.

items.label: Oxidation number
items.clue: The charge an atom would have if all its bonds were ionic.

items.label: Redox
items.clue: A reaction in which loss and gain of electrons happen together.

questions.stem: Chlorine reacts with aqueous iron(II) ions: 2Fe²⁺(aq) + Cl₂(aq) → 2Fe³⁺(aq) + 2Cl⁻(aq). Which species is the oxidising agent in this reaction?

options.text: Fe²⁺, since it loses electrons and so is itself oxidised
Cl₂, since it gains electrons and so is itself reduced
Cl⁻, since it is the species holding the gained electrons
None, since no species here gains or loses any oxygen atoms

questions.explanation: Chlorine's oxidation number falls from 0 to −1: each Cl₂ gains two electrons from Fe²⁺. The species that accepts electrons is the oxidising agent.

questions.stem: What are the oxidation numbers of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, and of oxygen in sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
questions.explanation: In NaH, Na is +1, so H is −1 (the hydride ion). In Na₂O₂, 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so O is −1 (the peroxide ion, O₂²⁻).

questions.stem: In acidic solution, MnO₄⁻(aq) is reduced to Mn²⁺(aq) and Fe²⁺(aq) is oxidised to Fe³⁺(aq). In the balanced overall redox equation, what amount of Fe²⁺ reacts with 1 mol of MnO₄⁻?
questions.explanation: Mn goes from +7 to +2, so each MnO₄⁻ gains 5 electrons; each Fe²⁺ loses 1. The iron half-equation is multiplied by 5.
2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = +12, so each Cr is +6. The numeral is per atom.
O in H₂O₂ is −1 (a peroxide). It goes to −2 in H₂O (reduced) and to 0 in O₂ (oxidised): one element in one species, both ways.

questions.stem: Chlorine is −1 in the chloride ion, Cl⁻, but +1 in the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻ (in bleach). Which explains the +1?

options.text: The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ has lost a proton to the oxygen atom, leaving chlorine with a +1 charge.
Oxygen always has the oxidation number −1 in an ion with one negative charge.
Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so it is assigned the shared electrons in the Cl–O bond.
The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ carries a real charge of +1, as in a Cl⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: O takes both shared electrons and is −2; the total must be −1, so x + (−2) = −1 and Cl is +1. In Cl⁻, chlorine holds an extra electron: −1.

questions.stem: In the thermite reaction, aluminium reacts with iron(III) oxide: Fe₂O₃(s) + 2Al(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(l). What happens to the iron?

options.text: It loses electrons: iron is always oxidised when it reacts, as it does in rusting.
It gains electrons: its oxidation number falls from +3 to 0, and aluminium supplies them.
It loses electrons to aluminium, since aluminium gains the oxygen during the reaction.
It gains electrons: its oxidation number falls from +6 to 0, as Fe₂O₃ has two Fe atoms.
